Verify Now Blog > PCB Layout Guidelines for Special Component Placement PCB Layout Guidelines for Special Component Placement by: Mila Oct 26,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout PCB layout is not an arbitrary process. It must follow certain design rules to ensure electrical performance, thermal management, and assembly quality. In addition to general layout requirements, some components have specific placement constraints that must be considered during PCB component placement. 1. Placement Requirements for Press-Fit Components For right-angle male and female press-fit components, no components taller than 3 mm should be placed within 3 mm of the component, and no soldered components should be placed within 1.5 mm. On the opposite side of the PCB, no components should be placed within 2.5 mm of the center of the press-fit pin holes. For straight male and female press-fit components, no components should be placed within 1 mm of the component. If a protective sleeve is required on the opposite side of the PCB, no components should be placed within 1 mm of the sleeve edge. If no sleeve is installed, no components should be placed within 2.5 mm of the press-fit holes. For hot-plug sockets used with grounding connectors in European-style connectors, components should not be placed within 6.5 mm of the front end of long pins or within 2.0 mm of the front end of short pins. For long pins on 2 mm FB single-pin power connectors, no components should be placed within 8 mm in front of the corresponding board-mounted socket. （Press-Fit Connector Placement and Clearance Requirements） 2. Placement Requirements for Temperature-Sensitive Components During PCB component placement, temperature-sensitive components should be kept away from high-heat components whenever possible. For example, electrolytic capacitors should be protected from prolonged exposure to excessive temperatures, while crystal oscillators require attention to temperature variations that may affect frequency stability. Components used for temperature sensing should be placed according to the target being measured and the actual heat-transfer path. They should be positioned to accurately reflect the target temperature while minimizing the influence of other heat-generating components, which could otherwise cause measurement errors or false triggering. Heat-generating components that can withstand high temperatures should be placed in locations that support effective heat dissipation, taking the actual airflow path into account. Components with limited heat resistance should be kept away from high-temperature areas. Where possible, avoid placing them directly in the airflow path downstream of other heat-generating components or where they may affect temperature-sensitive components. （PCB Layout for Thermal-Sensitive Components） 3. Placement Requirements for Polarized Components Through-hole devices (THD) with polarity or directional requirements should be oriented consistently and arranged neatly to facilitate insertion, soldering, and visual inspection. Surface-mount components (SMC) with polarity should preferably have a consistent orientation, provided that electrical connections and routing requirements are met. Components of the same type should be arranged neatly to simplify assembly and inspection. Common polarized components include electrolytic capacitors, tantalum capacitors, and diodes. During PCB layout, always verify component polarity markings against the schematic and PCB footprint to prevent circuit malfunctions caused by incorrect orientation. （Polarized Component Orientation in PCB Layout） 4. Placement Requirements for Through-Hole Reflow Components For PCBs with a dimension greater than 300 mm along the non-conveying edge, the placement of heavier components should be planned carefully, taking into account board thickness, support conditions, and component weight. Where appropriate, avoid placing heavy components in the center of the board to reduce the risk of PCB deformation and interference with component insertion or previously placed components. To facilitate component insertion, components may be placed closer to the insertion operation side, depending on the actual assembly process and equipment requirements. For long components, such as memory module sockets, the component's longitudinal axis should preferably be parallel to the PCB conveying direction, subject to the requirements of the production equipment and assembly process. The distance between the pad edges of through-hole reflow components and nearby QFPs, SOPs, connectors with a pitch of 0.65 mm or less, and all BGAs should be greater than 20 mm. The distance from other SMT components should be greater than 2 mm. These clearances should be verified against the actual soldering process and assembly manufacturer's requirements. The distance between the bodies of through-hole reflow components should be greater than 10 mm, subject to component dimensions and assembly process requirements. The distance between the pad edges of through-hole reflow components and the PCB conveying edge should be at least 10 mm. The distance from a non-conveying edge should be at least 5 mm. The design should also account for clamping areas, panelization, and production equipment constraints. Conclusion Proper PCB layout affects not only electrical performance but also thermal management, assembly efficiency, and product reliability. When developing PCB component placement guidelines, designers should consider component characteristics, electrical requirements, mechanical clearances, and manufacturing processes. Reviewing these factors against component datasheets and assembly requirements can help prevent placement conflicts, reduce manufacturing issues, and improve overall PCB design quality.
